tour.title: The Agent Loop
tour.description: Start at REEAgent, the top-level class in ree_core/agent.py that is the whole V3 cognitive architecture wired into one place. It runs a multi-rate sense-predict-select-act-residue loop, pulling together the latent stack, the E1/E2/E3 predictors, and the hippocampal, residue, affect, PFC and sleep subsystems. Everything else in this tour is something agent.py imports and calls, so read it as the map rather than the territory -- with 72 outgoing dependencies it is by far the highest-fan-out module in ree_core.
tour.languageLesson: Python has no header files, so a module this central becomes the de-facto architecture document. Reading the import block at the top of agent.py gives you the subsystem inventory in one screen before you read a single line of logic.

tour.title: Configuration Surface
tour.description: Before any subsystem makes sense you need the vocabulary of knobs it is built from. ree_core/utils/config.py is the single canonical configuration surface for every component -- latent stack, predictors, event segmenter, hippocampal subsystem, residue, heartbeat and environment -- aggregated by a top-level REEConfig with size presets and derived-dimension factories. With 12 modules importing it, it is the second most depended-upon file in the substrate, and a new substrate feature is almost always a new dataclass field here first.
tour.languageLesson: Python dataclasses with factory defaults let a config tree be both declarative and derived: a field like a latent dimension can be computed from its siblings at construction time, so callers get one consistent object instead of recomputing shapes everywhere.

tour.title: The Latent Stack (L-space)
tour.description: The latent stack is the representational floor the rest of the architecture stands on. It implements the split encoder that separates z_self from z_world, the shared beta/theta/delta multi-timescale depth stack, the harm/resource/affective-harm encoders, and the reafference and adversarial-split heads. Every predictor in Step 4 consumes these latents, and the residue field in Step 6 is literally a function over z_world -- so the shape of this module constrains what the whole agent can represent.

tour.title: E1/E2 Forward Models
tour.description: Prediction in V3 is split by timescale and by what is being predicted. E1 is the long-horizon substrate: a cue-indexed context bank plus an LSTM transition model with cue-context, action and terrain heads. E2 is the fast layer, and it is deliberately plural -- separate forward models for self, world state, world uncertainty, and two distinct harm channels (affective-pain and sensory-discriminative). The split matters scientifically: the affective-pain prediction error becomes the control-demand signal that dACC consumes in Step 8.

tour.title: E3 Selection and Goals
tour.description: E3 is where prediction turns into action. The selector scores candidate trajectories over z_world using harm evaluation, goal error and residue cost, and owns a dynamic precision derived from its own prediction-error variance -- making it the primary action-selection and commitment locus of the substrate. Its goal error term comes from z_goal, a slow-decay attractor in z_world space with an incentive-salience token bank and a cross-episode goal-anchor store. Nearly every PFC and cingulate module later in this tour reaches the behaviour only by biasing E3's scores.

tour.title: Residue: Non-Erasable Cost
tour.description: The residue field is the ethical core of the architecture and the concept that gives REE its name. It is an RBF-based, non-erasable accumulation of the cost of world-changes the agent caused, paired with a benefit terrain of positive attractors. Non-erasable is the design decision worth pausing on: unlike a reward signal that can be optimised away, residue persists as terrain and is read back as a cost term by E3 (Step 5) and as navigable terrain by the hippocampal planner (Step 7).

tour.title: Hippocampal Planning and Memory
tour.description: The hippocampal module runs a CEM search over action-object space rather than raw z_world, producing value-flat trajectory proposals that E3 then scores. Around it sit the pieces that give that search structure: a per-tick hierarchical event segmenter emitting outer.inner segment IDs, a scale-tagged anchor store with dual-trace preservation keyed by those boundary events, a staleness accumulator, and a ghost-goal bank. This cluster is tightly coupled by design -- the segmenter's boundaries are what install and remap anchors, and anchor staleness is what the sleep replay sampler in Step 10 draws from.

tour.title: Cingulate Control and Mode
tour.description: The cingulate cluster decides what kind of processing the agent should be doing at all. The salience coordinator binds the dACC, AIC, PCC and pACC subdivisions into one network and emits a soft probability vector over external_task, internal_planning, internal_replay and offline_consolidation, plus a mode-switch trigger. dACC itself is explicitly an integrator rather than a selector: it bundles expected value, choice difficulty, foraging value and the precision-weighted affective pain prediction error from Step 4's E2 harm model, and an adapter converts that bundle into per-candidate bias for E3.

tour.title: PFC Analogs and Commitment
tour.description: The PFC layer supplies the slow, rule-like control that keeps behaviour coherent across ticks. Lateral PFC holds a mode-conditioned persistent rule_state that becomes an additive per-candidate score bias; OFC contributes state-code and devaluation bias heads with the devaluation path deliberately decoupled from discrimination; frontopolar handles de-commit. Alongside them the policy layer decides when a chosen trajectory becomes a commitment, via a motor-program readiness signal feeding a commit-entry conjunction inside REEAgent.select_action. Note the recurring pattern: none of these modules act directly -- they all express themselves as bias into E3.

tour.title: Sleep and Offline Integration
tour.description: Sleep in V3 is a first-class computational phase, not downtime. The phase manager tracks episodes and waking steps, decides when to enter sleep behind an override-gated onset permit, and orchestrates the SWS/REM/writeback walk across the replay sampler, routing gate, Bayesian and self-model aggregators, and cross-module consolidator. The replay sampler draws anchors from a frozen staleness snapshot -- the staleness that Step 7's hippocampal cluster accumulated during waking -- and a Model Error Load consumer adapts sleep duration and entry timing to how much learning demand has built up.

tour.title: Affect, Attribution, Regulators
tour.description: A layer of slow regulators shapes everything above without being part of any single pathway. The harm-suffering accumulator converts the medium-timescale unpleasantness channel into a controllability-gated suffering load; the blocked-agency stream accumulates when intended actions are repeatedly blocked while goal and capacity-belief are retained; the amygdala analog turns affective harm into arousal-dependent encoding gain and retrieval bias. Attribution is the bridge between wake and sleep: the waking buffer records counterfactual-backed credit attributions that Step 10's Bayesian aggregator consumes offline. Many of these, like tonic serotonin, are default-off behind a master switch.
tour.languageLesson: The default-off master-switch pattern is how this repo ships experimental substrate safely: a module is imported and wired unconditionally, but its effect is multiplied by a config flag defaulting to disabled, so enabling it is a one-line experiment rather than a code change.

tour.title: Preservation and Reproducibility
tour.description: Because REE is a research programme, a run has to be reproducible from its inputs alone. The reconstruction record is an immutable, integrity-hashed bundle of the exact config, seed, environment, provenance and understanding needed to deterministically reproduce one REE life, with faithful REEConfig JSON round-tripping and append-only persistence. This is why Step 2's config module is written to be serialisable rather than merely convenient -- the config is part of the scientific record.

tour.title: The Coordination Database
tour.description: The tour now leaves the agent and enters the infrastructure that runs experiments across a fleet. schema.sql is idempotent SQLite DDL applied at coordinator startup, defining the 16 tables that back the Phase-3 coordination plane: the experiment queue and results, per-machine heartbeats and the command channel, and the git-mirrored registries for task claims, chips and workspace-state appends. Reading the tables first makes the Python in Step 14 far easier -- every endpoint there is a read or write against one of these.
tour.languageLesson: Idempotent DDL (CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, plus additive migrations) lets a schema file double as a migration runner: startup can apply it unconditionally on a fresh or existing database, which is what makes a new worker box self-provisioning.

tour.title: Coordinator Service and Sync
tour.description: Three modules sit on top of that schema. db.py is the SQLite persistence layer -- schema migrations, atomic experiment-claim arbitration, machine heartbeats, and the authoritative claim/chip/workspace-state registries -- and with 28 incoming dependencies it is the single most depended-upon file in the whole graph. app.py wraps it in a stdlib-only, bearer-token-authenticated HTTP API, and sync_daemon.py is the Phase-3 writer that makes the database, not git, the source of truth for coordination data. The atomic arbitration in db.py is the point: it is what stops two machines claiming the same experiment.

tour.title: Operating the Fleet
tour.description: Finish with the two documents that explain why the infrastructure is shaped the way it is. The cutover plan is the plan-of-record for making sync_daemon the sole git writer for coordination data, with env knobs, preconditions, human gates, verification, rollback and an explicit do-not-enable list. The operator guide gives the three-system mental model -- git heartbeats versus coordinator DB versus sync_daemon -- and troubleshooting recipes for writer conflicts and drift. Read together they turn Steps 13 and 14 from code you have seen into a system you could actually run.
